questions.prompt: Why should windows.pslist and windows.psscan always be run as a pair rather than relying on just one?
options: They always return identical results, so running both is just a formality
pslist walks a linked list that a hidden process can be unlinked from, while psscan scans memory directly for the EPROCESS pool tag and finds processes regardless of linkage
psscan is faster and pslist is only needed for older Windows versions
pslist only works on crash dumps, not live captures
questions.explanation: pslist walks ActiveProcessLinks, which a hidden process can be unlinked from via DKOM. psscan finds every EPROCESS-shaped structure in memory by its pool tag, regardless of list linkage -- any process psscan finds that pslist doesn't is a high-priority finding.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when windows.ldrmodules shows a DLL mapped in memory that's absent from that process's own dlllist output?
options: This is a normal, expected occurrence with no investigative significance
A strong signal of reflective loading or deliberate module-list tampering
The DLL has simply not finished loading yet
dlllist and ldrmodules always show identical results by design
questions.explanation: dlllist reads a process's own self-reported module list from its PEB, while ldrmodules cross-references that against actual mapped memory. A mismatch suggests something was loaded in a way that bypassed the normal, self-reporting mechanism.

questions.prompt: Why is windows.cmdline valuable even when process-creation logging (like Sysmon Event ID 1 or 4688) was enabled?
options: It's never actually useful if logging was already enabled
It can confirm the log entry and the live memory state actually agree, and recovers command lines even if logs have since rotated out of retention
cmdline only works when logging was disabled
It replaces the need for any event log analysis entirely
questions.explanation: Recovering command lines directly from memory provides an independent cross-check against log-based evidence, and remains available even after logs have aged out of retention.

questions.prompt: What does windows.pstree add that windows.pslist alone does not?
options: pstree shows completely different processes than pslist
The same process data, rendered as a parent-child tree, useful for spotting the wrong-parent red flags covered elsewhere in this academy
pstree requires a live system and cannot be used on a memory image
questions.explanation: pstree uses the same underlying data as pslist but renders it as a tree, making parent-child relationship anomalies (like the ones covered in Level 2's LOLBins content) directly visible.
